fetched_contents.text: Progressing the Progress Note for COPD Dear Editor: Electronic medical records (EMRs) can either improve medical care or impede it (i.e., “garbage in equals garbage out”). The ability to take a vast amount of material and methodically and meticulously extract the essential information is a skill for which medical documentation is long overdue. Since the development of the subjective-objective- assessment-plan (SOAP) note in the 1960’s by Lawrence Weed, MD, little has changed in the way physicians write a progress note.1 While EMRs dramatically improved the access and legibility of physicians’ notes, it also compounded the problem by giving physicians an easy way to overpopulate their notes with bulky and wordy results of diagnostic testing.2 By the same token, excluding this information leaves the reader to the unhappy task of reviewing endless PDF files on their own. In response to this need, I propose an overhaul to the assessment/plan portion of the SOAP note. By adding a goal-oriented scientific survey (GOSS or GO-SOAP) of the patient, this will not only accurately describe a patient’s condition and disease state, but also integrate evidence-based medicine into the everyday practice of medicine. This adds an artificial intelligence to an otherwise historical record. For example, the following is a SOAP note assessment and plan with a goal-oriented scientific survey (GOSS note) for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD): SOAP Assessment/Plan:COPD- Patient has increased shortness of breath today. Will increase bronchodilators and repeat chest X-ray. Will give empiric trial of steroids and antibiotics for acute exacerbation. Patient to follow-up in 1 week. GOSS Assessment/Plan:a COPD, Gold 2B. 3 Tobacco: 40 pack years. Off cigarettes. Continue smoking cessation. CAT score4 (Dec 2015): 12 PFTs (Dec 2015): FEV1 1.77 L, 78%. FEV1 decline < 40 mL per year. 6MWT (Dec 2015): 412 meters, without desaturation CPST (Oct 2014): VO2 max 12 ml/kg/min. Patient enrolled in Pulmonary Rehab. CT chest (Feb 2015): RLL nodule, enrolled in lung cancer screening program Alpha-1 level (Sept 2013): normal, MM Vaccines: She has had a pneumonia vaccine (2013) and will need booster age 70. She has had a pertussis (2012) and influenza vaccine. Failed: Inhaled steroids- paradoxical bronchospasm Treatment: Now with acute exacerbation, will give antibiotics and oral steroids. Increase SABA to qid and prn. Will consider a trial of PDE inhibitors as patient has had repeat exacerbations this year. Will be due to follow-up PFTs in Dec 2016. Exacerbations: Oct 2012 Hospitalized with antibiotics and steroids Jan 2015 BAL with staphylococcus, treated with antibiotics Mar 2015 ED treated with antibiotics and steroids Advanced directives: Full Code, agrees to trach/PEG if needed. NOK is Husband with cell phone 999-999-9999; GOLD=Global initiative for chronic Obstructive Lung Disease; CAT=COPD Assessment Test; PFTs=pulmonary function tests;forced expiratory volume in 1 second=FEV1 6MWTs=6-Minute Walk Test; CPST=cardiopulmonary stress test; CT=computed tomography; SABA=short-acting beta2-agonists; qid=4 times per day ; prn=use when necessary;PDE=phosphodiesterase; BAL=bronchoalveolar lavage; ED=emergency department; PEG=percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy; NOK=next of kin a please note: patent pending In this note, the patient has met the goal for smoking cessation, but may not be at goal for the number of exacerbations per year. The objective evaluation is using the pulmonary function testing and Global initiative for chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) classification to decide on medications and the enrollment into pulmonary rehabilitation. The subjective survey is the inclusion of the CAT score and/or other validated surveys to quantify patient symptoms instead of self-reporting. In conclusion, while this form of documentation in the assessment/plan note section may initially seem cumbersome, it can greatly reduce the need to rummage through a large stack of electronic and paper records. Overall, this will reduce the time needed to evaluate and manage each patient. It serves to allow for quick comparison to prior visits, reminders for necessary screenings and follow-up evaluations, keeping track of the past successes and failures in management, as well as allowing for new avenues which have not yet been explored. However, the beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Physicians must decide for themselves what they feel would best belong in their own note. This is just a simple proposal to show a glimpse of the possibilities for a more interesting and useful medical record. fetched_contents.text: LABA/LAMA as First-Line Therapy for COPD: A Summary of the Evidence and Guideline Recommendations Abstract Inhaled bronchodilators (alone or in combination) are the cornerstone of treatment for symptomatic patients with COPD, either as initial/first-line treatment or for second-line/treatment escalation in patients who experience persistent symptoms or exacerbations on monotherapy. The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease 2022 report recommends initial pharmacological treatment with a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) or a long-acting β2-agonist (LABA) as monotherapy for most patients, or dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA) in patients with more severe symptoms, regardless of exacerbation history. The recommendations for LABA/LAMA are broader in the American Thoracic Society treatment guidelines, which strongly recommend LABA/LAMA combination therapy over LAMA or LABA monotherapy in patients with COPD and dyspnea or exercise intolerance. However, despite consistent guideline recommendations, real-world prescribing data indicate that LAMA and/or LABA without an inhaled corticosteroid are not the most widely prescribed therapies in COPD. This article reviews global and regional/national guideline recommendations for the use of LABA/LAMA in COPD, examines the evidence for the effectiveness and safety of LABA/LAMA versus other therapies and offers a practical guide for clinicians to help ensure appropriate use of LABA/LAMA therapy. Keywords: COPD, LABA/LAMA, bronchodilator, inhaled corticosteroid 1. Introduction Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airflow limitation and persistent respiratory symptoms (most commonly dyspnea, cough and/or sputum production) and is punctuated by periods of acute worsening, known as exacerbations [1]. Chronic and progressive dyspnea is the most characteristic and debilitating symptom of COPD [1,2]. Activity-related dyspnea has a profound impact on patients’ lives, preventing them from participating in physical activity and often leading to the adoption of a sedentary lifestyle in order to cope with symptoms [3,4,5]. Inhaled bronchodilators (alone or in combination) have become the cornerstone of treatment for symptomatic patients with COPD, either as initial/first-line treatment or for second-line treatment in patients with persistent symptoms or exacerbations despite monotherapy [1,6,7,8]. The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) 2022 report recommends initial pharmacological treatment with a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) or a long-acting β2-agonist (LABA) for the majority of patients, and dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA) in patients with more severe symptoms, regardless of exacerbation history [1]. The second-line use of LABA/LAMA is recommended for patients who remain symptomatic despite monotherapy and for those who continue to have exacerbations but are not indicated for add-on therapy with an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) [1]. A list of currently approved fixed-dose LABA/LAMA combinations is provided in Table 1. The optimal components for LABA/LAMA combination therapy are not considered further in this review but are discussed elsewhere [9,10,11]. Table 1. Fixed-dose combinations of LABAs and LAMAs currently approved for COPD treatment [12]. fetched_contents.text: American Thoracic Society An exacerbation (ex-zass-cer-bay-shun) of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a worsening or “flare up” of your COPD symptoms. In many cases an exacerbation is caused by an infection in the lungs, but in some cases, the cause is never known. The inflammation (irritation and swelling) in the lungs during and after an exacerbation can cause some people to be extremely ill and it often takes a month or longer to recover completely. Knowing the signs and symptoms of an exacerbation will help you to get treatment early, shorten the length of the exacerbation, and hopefully prevent the exacerbation from becoming severe. What Causes an Exacerbation? The most common cause of an exacerbation is infection in the lungs or airways (breathing tubes). This infection is often from a virus, but it may also be caused by bacteria or less common types of organisms. Exacerbations can also occur from inhaling irritating substances from the environment like air pollution, or from severe allergies. The lungs react to infection or irritating substances by developing inflammation that makes the airways narrow from muscle tightness, swelling, and mucus (see Figure 2). These changes in the airways cause the increased signs and symptoms. For more about COPD see other ATS Patient Information Series pieces. What Are the Signs and Symptoms of an Exacerbation? * You may notice that you become more breathless than usual with routine activities, like walking to the car or showering. * Exacerbations can come on very quickly (hours to days). They involve worsening of your usual signs and symptoms of COPD * Your typical cough may increase in severity or frequency, or a new cough may develop. You may notice a change in the color of your sputum (mucus) from clear to colored (deep yellow, green, or brown) and/or the amount of sputum that you bring up may increase. In many people, a change in sputum is the first sign that they have an exacerbation. * You may feel more tired (fatigue). * If you find that you have more trouble sleeping than usual, develop a headache when you wake up, or feel confused (or a family member notices that you are confused and/or has difficulty waking you up), you may be having signs of high carbon dioxide levels that need immediate medical attention. * If you measure your oxygen level regularly by using a pulse oximeter, you may also notice that your oxygen levels are lower than usual. * You can also have other signs and symptoms of infections in the lung, such as fever. You should report the signs and symptoms you notice to your health care provider to figure out if you are having an exacerbation and how it should be treated. If you have had an exacerbation of your COPD in the past, you should take note of the “pattern” of your symptoms. Everyone has slightly different signs and symptoms from an exacerbation. In particular, notice the color and amount of sputum you bring up every day when you are not ill so that you recognize your signs and symptoms of an exacerbation. How Is an Exacerbation Diagnosed? Diagnosis of an exacerbation is based upon a history of worsened signs (such as your oxygen levels being lower than normal for you) and symptoms and physical exam findings by a provider. You may feel like you cannot get a big enough breath, are wheezing, or experience rapid shallow breathing. There are no tests of the blood, sputum, or chest x-rays that have been found to diagnose an exacerbation. Thus, the best person to help identify an exacerbation early is you. Knowing the signs and symptoms of an exacerbation and getting help early are the very best ways to limit it from becoming very severe. How Is an Exacerbation Treated? Some exacerbations can be treated at home with inhalers, steroids, and/or antibiotics. However, if your symptoms become severe, you will need to be hospitalized. Treatment of an exacerbation is primarily with medications to control the swelling and constriction (tightness) in your airways. The airway swelling is treated with steroid pills or IV (intravenous) steroids. Airway constriction is treated with bronchodilators such as an inhaler or nebulizer. In most cases, you will also be prescribed an antibiotic to treat bacterial infection. The main function of your lungs is to supply oxygen to the body and rid the body of carbon dioxide. Exacerbations can interfere with this, so you may need to have extra oxygen. You may need support from a PAP (positive airway pressure) machine with a nose or facemask to help you breathe better. If your exacerbation is severe, you may need treatment in an intensive care unit (ICU) and require a mechanical ventilator (a machine to breathe for you). How Serious Is an Exacerbation? Exacerbations can be very serious and can lead to death. Getting help early is therefore very important. This is known as an Action Plan and is described below. It is difficult to know who will get an exacerbation; however, if you have had one in the past, you have a greater chance of having another. SOAP note structure and template framework

A standard SOAP note is organized into four sections: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan (SOAP). The evidence here supports a goal-oriented scientific survey (GOSS) extension of the traditional SOAP note, which can help organize a COPD assessment more systematically by linking symptoms, diagnostics, and treatment decisions [N1-F1]. For a new COPD patient, the template should be adapted to capture COPD-specific elements such as GOLD classification, exacerbation risk, current disease control, comorbidities, and medication use, while also including functional status and home monitoring cues [N1-R3].

In the **Subjective** section, the patient’s chief complaint, symptoms, and concerns should be captured in detail. For a COPD patient, this includes dyspnea, breathlessness, cough, sputum changes, and any new or worsening symptoms [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The evidence also suggests asking about dyspnea triggers and what activities bring on shortness of breath, which is useful for identifying functional limitations and exacerbation risk [N2-R3]. A new patient’s history should also include smoking history, occupational exposures, and any prior COPD diagnosis or treatment [N1-F1].

In the **Objective** section, the note should record physical findings, vital signs, spirometry or pulmonary function test results, oxygen saturation, and any abnormal respiratory signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]. For COPD, oxygen saturation is especially important because the assessment/plan in the cited example notes that worsening signs such as lower oxygen levels than normal can be part of exacerbation recognition [N1-F1]. The evidence also supports including spirometry values, PFTs, 6MWT, and CAT score, which help quantify disease severity and response to treatment [N1-F1].

In the **Assessment** section, the note should integrate the clinical findings into a diagnosis and disease staging. The cited COPD-specific SOAP/GOSS note example uses GOLD classification, CAT score, PFTs, and other validated surveys to quantify symptoms and guide medication decisions [N1-F1]. This is directly relevant to a new COPD patient’s assessment because GOLD classification helps determine treatment level, and the CAT score helps measure symptom burden and disease control [N1-F1]. The assessment should also identify whether the patient’s symptoms are worsening, whether exacerbation risk is elevated, and whether there are signs of acute decompensation [N1-R3][N1-F1].

In the **Plan** section, the note should outline treatment, monitoring, education, and follow-up. The evidence supports a plan that corresponds with the diagnosis and includes both home management and escalation cues [N2-R2]. The cited example also shows that the plan can include increasing bronchodilators, repeating chest X-ray, empiric steroids and antibiotics for acute exacerbation, follow-up in 1 week, and follow-up PFTs [N1-F1]. For a new COPD patient, the plan should also include rescue medication review, inhaler instructions, oxygen therapy guidance, and next steps for when symptoms worsen [N1-R1][N1-F1].

Overall, the SOAP note template should be adapted for a new COPD patient by placing GOLD classification, exacerbation risk, current disease control, comorbidities, and functional status early in the note, and by anchoring the assessment and plan in objective findings such as oxygen saturation, spirometry, and symptom scores [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The physician’s assessment and plan should appear after the subjective and objective sections, with the assessment linking findings to a diagnosis and treatment level, and the plan specifying medications, monitoring, and escalation cues [N1-F1].

clinical assessment and history for a new COPD patient

For a new COPD patient, the clinical assessment should start with symptoms and severity indicators. The evidence emphasizes dyspnea as the most characteristic and debilitating symptom of COPD, with activity-related dyspnea having a major impact on functional status and quality of life [N3-F2]. Breathlessness should be assessed by asking when it occurs, what activities bring it on, and how severe it is [N2-R3]. The evidence also supports a thorough assessment of breathlessness because dyspnea is complex and requires careful evaluation for accurate diagnosis and effective management [N2-R2]. For a new patient, this means recording both current dyspnea and any new or worsening symptoms, including changes in sputum production, sputum color, or cough frequency [N4-F3].

Functional status and activity limitation are central to COPD assessment. The cited evidence notes that activity-related dyspnea prevents patients from participating in physical activity and can lead to a sedentary lifestyle [N3-F2]. A new COPD patient’s assessment should therefore include functional limitations, such as difficulty with routine activities, reduced exercise tolerance, and any impairment in daily living [N3-F2]. The evidence also supports using validated surveys to quantify symptoms instead of relying only on self-report, which can help assess functional status more objectively [N1-F1]. For example, the cited COPD SOAP note example includes a CAT score and 6MWT results to help quantify disease control and activity limitations [N1-F1].

Medication use and adherence issues are important because COPD treatment depends on inhaled therapy, and poor adherence can worsen symptoms and exacerbation risk. The evidence shows that rescue bronchodilator therapy is recommended for all patients with stable COPD, and that inhaled therapies should be optimized [N3-R2]. It also emphasizes that medication use should be reviewed for adherence and appropriateness [N3-R3]. For a new patient, the history should include current inhalers, rescue medications, and any history of medication changes or non-adherence [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The evidence also indicates that real-world prescribing patterns may differ from guideline recommendations, so the history should be used to identify whether the patient is on a guideline-recommended regimen or whether adjustments are needed [N3-F2].

In summary, the clinical assessment for a new COPD patient should capture dyspnea severity and triggers, functional limitations, and medication use, while also documenting any signs of worsening symptoms that may indicate exacerbation risk [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-F2]. The assessment should be structured around the patient’s ability to perform daily activities, their response to current therapy, and any gaps in adherence or medication appropriateness [N3-R2][N3-R3]. This foundation supports a targeted clinical decision and treatment plan [N1-F1].

follow-up and patient education planning

Follow-up and patient education planning should focus on trigger avoidance, home monitoring, and clear next steps for when symptoms worsen. The evidence supports patient education on when to seek medical attention for exacerbations as a vital part of COPD management [N5-R3]. It also states that self-management interventions are associated with fewer exacerbations and hospitalizations, highlighting the importance of a structured follow-up plan [N5-R1]. For a COPD patient, education should cover both routine follow-up and acute warning signs [N5-R3].

Trigger avoidance is a key component of COPD management. The evidence indicates that COPD self-management interventions can reduce exacerbations and that patients should learn the signs of exacerbation or flare-up and how to reduce exposure to triggers [N5-R2]. The evidence also notes that COPD exacerbations can be caused by infection in the lungs or airways, as well as by inhaling irritating substances like air pollution or severe allergens [N4-F3]. Therefore, patient education should include avoiding tobacco smoke, secondhand smoke, allergens, and environmental pollutants, and using a clean environment to reduce symptom triggers [N4-F3][N5-R2].

Home monitoring is essential for early detection of worsening disease. The evidence emphasizes routine follow-ups and monitoring key clinical indicators, including spirometry values and changes in symptoms [N5-R4]. It also supports oxygen saturation monitoring as part of exacerbation recognition, since worsening signs such as lower oxygen levels than normal can signal an exacerbation [N1-F1]. The cited COPD exacerbation guidance notes that patients may measure oxygen levels regularly with a pulse oximeter and that lower-than-usual levels may indicate a worsening situation [N4-F3]. For a new COPD patient, the home monitoring plan should include regular oxygen saturation checks, symptom tracking, and a clear plan for when to contact the provider [N4-F3][N5-R4].

The evidence notes that patients should be taught to report symptoms early, know their pattern of exacerbation signs, and understand what steps to take when symptoms get worse [N4-F3]. The patient should be taught to recognize exacerbation signs, know when to seek medical help, and understand the importance of adherence to follow-up and home monitoring [N5-R3][N4-F3].

medication review and treatment recommendations for COPD

The evidence supports a clear distinction between inhaler classes, rescue medications, and COPD-specific treatment guidance. For inhalers, the evidence emphasizes that inhaled bronchodilators are the cornerstone of COPD treatment, either as initial/first-line treatment or for second-line treatment in patients with persistent symptoms or exacerbations [N3-F2]. It also notes that long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) and long-acting β2-agonists (LABAs) are important bronchodilator classes, with dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA) being recommended in patients with more severe symptoms [N3-F2]. Rescue medication review is also important because the evidence states that rescue bronchodilator therapy is recommended for all patients with stable COPD [N3-R2].

GOLD/ICS/LABA/LAMA guidance is central to COPD treatment. The evidence shows that the GOLD 2022 report recommends initial pharmacological treatment with a LAMA or LABA for most patients, and dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA) for patients with more severe symptoms, regardless of exacerbation history [N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that the American Thoracic Society (ATS) guidelines strongly recommend LABA/LAMA combination therapy over LAMA or LABA monotherapy in patients with COPD and dyspnea or exercise intolerance [N3-F2]. This indicates that GOLD and ATS guidance are broadly aligned on the importance of dual bronchodilator therapy for symptomatic patients [N3-F2].

When to limit or avoid ICS and which combinations are preferred is a key point. The evidence states that ICS-containing combinations should be reserved for a specific subgroup of patients: those with a high eosinophil count (≥300 cells/μL), a history of frequent exacerbations (≥2 moderate exacerbations or 1 exacerbation leading to hospitalization in patients with ≥100 eosinophils/μL), or a history of asthma [N3-F2]. It also notes that ICS use may be over-prescribed in COPD because of perceived similarity with asthma or coexistence of the two conditions, and because physicians may focus more on exacerbation prevention than on symptom control [N3-F2]. Therefore, ICS should be limited or avoided in patients who do not meet these specific criteria [N3-F2].

The evidence also supports triple therapy as an escalation option. It states that triple therapy is recommended for patients not adequately controlled by existing inhaled combination therapies, and that LABA/LAMA can be escalated to triple therapy when appropriate [N3-R4][N3-R3]. The GOLD pocket guide evidence similarly supports triple therapy (LABA+LAMA+ICS) as a step-up in treatment when indicated [N6-R1]. However, the evidence also notes that real-world prescribing patterns may not always match guideline recommendations, so the review should include both the evidence-based preference and the practical consideration of current prescribing practices [N3-F2].

In summary, the medication review and treatment recommendations for COPD should emphasize bronchodilator use, rescue bronchodilator therapy, GOLD/ATS guidance for LAMA, LABA, and LABA/LAMA, and cautious use of ICS in patients who meet specific criteria [N3-F2][N3-R2]. Triple therapy should be considered when dual bronchodilator therapy is inadequate, but it should be reserved for patients who fit the evidence-based criteria for ICS-containing treatment [N3-R4][N3-F2].

## 2. Subjective section

### Chief complaint
- “Shortness of breath” or “dyspnea” is the primary concern [N2-R2][N2-R5].
- Other symptoms may include cough, sputum changes, fatigue, or worsening breathlessness with routine activities [N4-F3].

### History of present illness
- When did the shortness of breath start?
- How long has it lasted?
- Is it getting worse, or is it new?
- Are there changes in sputum production, color, or frequency?
- Any fever or other new symptoms?
- What activities bring on or worsen shortness of breath?
- Are there any recent infections or environmental exposures?
- Are there any medication changes, missed doses, or difficulty using inhalers?
- Any history of exacerbations, hospitalizations, or emergency visits?

### Past medical history
- COPD diagnosis, GOLD classification, and current disease control [N1-F1].
- History of asthma, eosinophilia, or frequent exacerbations [N3-F2].
- Comorbidities, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or others relevant to COPD management [N1-F1].

### Medication history
- Current inhalers, rescue medications, and any other prescribed medications [N3-R2][N3-R3].
- Adherence to current therapy, including missed doses or difficulty using devices [N3-R2][N3-R3].

### Smoking and exposures
- Tobacco use history, including pack-years and cessation status [N1-F1].
- Exposure to environmental irritants, allergens, or pollutants [N4-F3].

---

## 3. Objective section

### Vital signs
- Blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature, and oxygen saturation [N1-F1][N4-F3].
- Oxygen saturation should be recorded and compared to the patient’s baseline, especially if the provider suspects exacerbation [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### Physical examination
- Respiratory exam: wheezing, crackles, use of accessory muscles, respiratory distress, and altered mental status [N1-R1][N4-F3].
- Signs of hypercapnia: confusion, altered level of consciousness, or other indicators of respiratory failure [N4-F3].

### Pulmonary function and functional assessment
- Spirometry, PFTs, CAT score, and 6MWT results, if available [N1-F1].
- Any recent chest X-ray or other imaging relevant to the current episode [N1-F1].

### Laboratory or diagnostic findings
- Eosinophil count, if relevant to ICS eligibility [N3-F2].
- Other laboratory values that may affect management or exacerbation risk [N1-F1].

---

## 4. Assessment section

### Diagnosis and staging
- COPD with shortness of breath, likely worsening symptoms [N2-R2][N4-F3].
- GOLD classification and exacerbation risk status [N1-F1][N1-R3].
- Acute exacerbation suspicion if there is increased dyspnea, worsening sputum, or lower-than-usual oxygen levels [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### Severity and functional status
- Dyspnea severity and activity limitation should be quantified with validated tools rather than relying only on self-report [N1-F1][N2-R3].
- Functional limitation: reduced exercise tolerance, difficulty with routine activities, and impact on daily living [N3-F2].

### Medication review
- Current therapy should be evaluated for appropriateness, adherence, and any gaps [N3-R2][N3-R3].
- Rescue bronchodilator therapy should be checked, as it is recommended for all patients with stable COPD [N3-R2].

### Exacerbation risk
- Exacerbation risk is elevated if the patient has increased sputum production, changes in sputum color, or a history of frequent exacerbations [N4-F3].
- The patient may need an action plan for early recognition of worsening symptoms [N4-F3].

### Differential considerations
- Consider acute exacerbation, infection, or other respiratory causes if the clinical picture is unclear [N4-F3].

---

## 5. Plan section

### Treatment and medication plan
- **Inhalers and bronchodilators**: confirm current regimen and consider whether to optimize, escalate, or change therapy [N3-F2][N3-R2].
- **Rescue medication**: ensure the patient understands when and how to use rescue bronchodilators [N3-R2].
- **ICS use**: reserve ICS for patients with high eosinophil count, history of frequent exacerbations, or asthma [N3-F2]. Avoid ICS in patients who do not meet these criteria [N3-F2].
- **Triple therapy**: consider LABA/LAMA/ICS if dual bronchodilator therapy is inadequate [N3-R4][N6-R1].
- **Oxygen therapy**: titrate to achieve SaO2 >90% or PaO2 >60 mmHg, but avoid over-oxygenation in patients at risk for hypercapnia [N4-F3].

### Monitoring and follow-up
- Schedule follow-up in 1 week and arrange future PFTs or other monitoring as needed [N1-F1].
- Use routine follow-ups to ask about and monitor key clinical indicators, including spirometry values and changes in symptoms [N5-R4].

### Home monitoring plan
- Teach the patient to monitor oxygen saturation, symptom changes, and sputum characteristics [N4-F3][N5-R4].
- Provide a clear action plan for when symptoms worsen and what to do next [N4-F3].

### Patient education
- Educate on trigger avoidance, including tobacco smoke, allergens, air pollution, and environmental irritants [N4-F3][N5-R2].
- Teach the patient to recognize exacerbation signs and when to seek help [N5-R3][N4-F3].
- Emphasize adherence to prescribed medications and the importance of follow-up [N3-R2][N5-R4].

### Escalation cues
- Seek medical attention if there is worsening breathlessness, increased sputum, changes in sputum color, fever, confusion, altered mental status, or lower-than-usual oxygen levels [N4-F3].
- If symptoms become severe, consider hospitalization, IV steroids, nebulized bronchodilators, antibiotics, and oxygen support [N4-F3].
- The cited COPD SOAP note example includes empiric steroids and antibiotics for acute exacerbation, increasing bronchodilators, and follow-up in 1 week [N1-F1].

---

## 6. Sample COPD SOAP note template

### Subjective
- Chief complaint: Shortness of breath
- History of present illness: The patient reports worsening shortness of breath over the past [X] days. Symptoms are worse with routine activities, and they now notice increased cough and changes in sputum. They have no fever but feel more fatigued. They have been using their rescue inhaler more frequently.
- Past medical history: COPD, GOLD [X], previous exacerbations [X], asthma history [X], comorbidities [X].
- Medication history: Current inhalers include [X]. Rescue medication includes [X]. Adherence is [X].
- Smoking history: [X] pack-years, currently [X].
- Environmental exposures: [X].

### Objective
- Vital signs: BP [X], HR [X], RR [X], Temp [X], SaO2 [X]
- Respiratory exam: Wheezing, crackles, accessory muscle use, respiratory distress, confusion [X]
- Pulmonary function: CAT score [X], PFTs [X], 6MWT [X]
- Chest X-ray: [X]
- Other findings: [X]

### Assessment
- Diagnosis: COPD with worsening dyspnea
- GOLD classification: [X]
- Exacerbation risk: [X]
- Functional status: [X]
- Medication review: [X]
- Acute exacerbation suspicion: [X]
- Differential diagnosis: [X]

### Plan
- Inhalers/bronchodilators: [X]
- Rescue medication: [X]
- ICS use: [X]
- Triple therapy: [X]
- Oxygen therapy: [X]
- Follow-up: [X]
- Home monitoring: [X]
- Patient education: [X]
- Escalation cues: [X]

---

## 7. Clinical synthesis

This template is built on the branch reports’ evidence and should be tailored to the specific patient. For a new COPD patient, the note should emphasize:
- **Symptoms and severity indicators**: dyspnea, breathlessness, cough, sputum changes [N2-R2][N4-F3].
- **Functional status**: reduced exercise tolerance, difficulty with daily activities, and impact on quality of life [N3-F2].
- **Medication review**: current inhalers, rescue medications, adherence, and ICS eligibility [N3-R2][N3-F2].
- **Exacerbation recognition**: increased sputum, changes in sputum color, fatigue, confusion, and altered oxygen levels [N4-F3].
- **Oxygen management**: titrate to SaO2 >90% or PaO2 >60 mmHg, but be cautious of over-oxygenation [N4-F3].
- **Trigger avoidance and education**: teach the patient to avoid tobacco, allergens, and pollutants, and to recognize worsening signs [N4-F3][N5-R2].
- **Follow-up and escalation**: schedule routine follow-ups, teach home monitoring, and define clear next steps for worsening symptoms [N5-R4][N4-F3].

The evidence also supports using validated surveys and spirometry to quantify disease severity and response to treatment [N1-F1]. In practice, this SOAP note should be adapted to the patient’s baseline, exacerbation history, and current therapeutic context [N1-F1][N3-F2].

SOAP note structure and template framework

A standard SOAP note is organized into four sections: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan (SOAP). The evidence here supports a goal-oriented scientific survey (GOSS) extension of the traditional SOAP note, which can help organize a COPD assessment more systematically by linking symptoms, diagnostics, and treatment decisions [N1-F1]. For a new COPD patient, the template should be adapted to capture COPD-specific elements such as GOLD classification, exacerbation risk, current disease control, comorbidities, and medication use, while also including functional status and home monitoring cues [N1-R3].

In the **Subjective** section, the patient’s chief complaint, symptoms, and concerns should be captured in detail. For a COPD patient, this includes dyspnea, breathlessness, cough, sputum changes, and any new or worsening symptoms [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The evidence also suggests asking about dyspnea triggers and what activities bring on shortness of breath, which is useful for identifying functional limitations and exacerbation risk [N2-R3]. A new patient’s history should also include smoking history, occupational exposures, and any prior COPD diagnosis or treatment [N1-F1].

In the **Objective** section, the note should record physical findings, vital signs, spirometry or pulmonary function test results, oxygen saturation, and any abnormal respiratory signs [N1-R1][N1-F1]. For COPD, oxygen saturation is especially important because the assessment/plan in the cited example notes that worsening signs such as lower oxygen levels than normal can be part of exacerbation recognition [N1-F1]. The evidence also supports including spirometry values, PFTs, 6MWT, and CAT score, which help quantify disease severity and response to treatment [N1-F1].

In the **Assessment** section, the note should integrate the clinical findings into a diagnosis and disease staging. The cited COPD-specific SOAP/GOSS note example uses GOLD classification, CAT score, PFTs, and other validated surveys to quantify symptoms and guide medication decisions [N1-F1]. This is directly relevant to a new COPD patient’s assessment because GOLD classification helps determine treatment level, and the CAT score helps measure symptom burden and disease control [N1-F1]. The assessment should also identify whether the patient’s symptoms are worsening, whether exacerbation risk is elevated, and whether there are signs of acute decompensation [N1-R3][N1-F1].

In the **Plan** section, the note should outline treatment, monitoring, education, and follow-up. The evidence supports a plan that corresponds with the diagnosis and includes both home management and escalation cues [N2-R2]. The cited example also shows that the plan can include increasing bronchodilators, repeating chest X-ray, empiric steroids and antibiotics for acute exacerbation, follow-up in 1 week, and follow-up PFTs [N1-F1]. For a new COPD patient, the plan should also include rescue medication review, inhaler instructions, oxygen therapy guidance, and next steps for when symptoms worsen [N1-R1][N1-F1].

Overall, the SOAP note template should be adapted for a new COPD patient by placing GOLD classification, exacerbation risk, current disease control, comorbidities, and functional status early in the note, and by anchoring the assessment and plan in objective findings such as oxygen saturation, spirometry, and symptom scores [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The physician’s assessment and plan should appear after the subjective and objective sections, with the assessment linking findings to a diagnosis and treatment level, and the plan specifying medications, monitoring, and escalation cues [N1-F1].

clinical assessment and history for a new COPD patient

For a new COPD patient, the clinical assessment should start with symptoms and severity indicators. The evidence emphasizes dyspnea as the most characteristic and debilitating symptom of COPD, with activity-related dyspnea having a major impact on functional status and quality of life [N3-F2]. Breathlessness should be assessed by asking when it occurs, what activities bring it on, and how severe it is [N2-R3]. The evidence also supports a thorough assessment of breathlessness because dyspnea is complex and requires careful evaluation for accurate diagnosis and effective management [N2-R2]. For a new patient, this means recording both current dyspnea and any new or worsening symptoms, including changes in sputum production, sputum color, or cough frequency [N4-F3].

Functional status and activity limitation are central to COPD assessment. The cited evidence notes that activity-related dyspnea prevents patients from participating in physical activity and can lead to a sedentary lifestyle [N3-F2]. A new COPD patient’s assessment should therefore include functional limitations, such as difficulty with routine activities, reduced exercise tolerance, and any impairment in daily living [N3-F2]. The evidence also supports using validated surveys to quantify symptoms instead of relying only on self-report, which can help assess functional status more objectively [N1-F1]. For example, the cited COPD SOAP note example includes a CAT score and 6MWT results to help quantify disease control and activity limitations [N1-F1].

Medication use and adherence issues are important because COPD treatment depends on inhaled therapy, and poor adherence can worsen symptoms and exacerbation risk. The evidence shows that rescue bronchodilator therapy is recommended for all patients with stable COPD, and that inhaled therapies should be optimized [N3-R2]. It also emphasizes that medication use should be reviewed for adherence and appropriateness [N3-R3]. For a new patient, the history should include current inhalers, rescue medications, and any history of medication changes or non-adherence [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The evidence also indicates that real-world prescribing patterns may differ from guideline recommendations, so the history should be used to identify whether the patient is on a guideline-recommended regimen or whether adjustments are needed [N3-F2].

In summary, the clinical assessment for a new COPD patient should capture dyspnea severity and triggers, functional limitations, and medication use, while also documenting any signs of worsening symptoms that may indicate exacerbation risk [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-F2]. The assessment should be structured around the patient’s ability to perform daily activities, their response to current therapy, and any gaps in adherence or medication appropriateness [N3-R2][N3-R3]. This foundation supports a targeted clinical decision and treatment plan [N1-F1].

follow-up and patient education planning

Follow-up and patient education planning should focus on trigger avoidance, home monitoring, and clear next steps for when symptoms worsen. The evidence supports patient education on when to seek medical attention for exacerbations as a vital part of COPD management [N5-R3]. It also states that self-management interventions are associated with fewer exacerbations and hospitalizations, highlighting the importance of a structured follow-up plan [N5-R1]. For a COPD patient, education should cover both routine follow-up and acute warning signs [N5-R3].

Trigger avoidance is a key component of COPD management. The evidence indicates that COPD self-management interventions can reduce exacerbations and that patients should learn the signs of exacerbation or flare-up and how to reduce exposure to triggers [N5-R2]. The evidence also notes that COPD exacerbations can be caused by infection in the lungs or airways, as well as by inhaling irritating substances like air pollution or severe allergens [N4-F3]. Therefore, patient education should include avoiding tobacco smoke, secondhand smoke, allergens, and environmental pollutants, and using a clean environment to reduce symptom triggers [N4-F3][N5-R2].

Home monitoring is essential for early detection of worsening disease. The evidence emphasizes routine follow-ups and monitoring key clinical indicators, including spirometry values and changes in symptoms [N5-R4]. It also supports oxygen saturation monitoring as part of exacerbation recognition, since worsening signs such as lower oxygen levels than normal can signal an exacerbation [N1-F1]. The cited COPD exacerbation guidance notes that patients may measure oxygen levels regularly with a pulse oximeter and that lower-than-usual levels may indicate a worsening situation [N4-F3]. For a new COPD patient, the home monitoring plan should include regular oxygen saturation checks, symptom tracking, and a clear plan for when to contact the provider [N4-F3][N5-R4].

Next steps and when to seek help should be clearly defined in the plan. The evidence notes that patients should be taught to report symptoms early, know their pattern of exacerbation signs, and understand what steps to take when symptoms get worse [N4-F3]. It also states that if a patient has had an exacerbation before, they should be encouraged to discuss prevention and early management with their provider and to have an action plan [N4-F3]. For follow-up planning, the evidence supports routine follow-ups and using them to ask about and monitor key clinical indicators [N5-R4]. The COPD SOAP note example includes a follow-up in 1 week and future PFTs as part of the plan [N1-F1].

Overall, follow-up and patient education planning should center on avoiding triggers, monitoring symptoms and oxygen levels, and providing a clear action plan for worsening symptoms [N5-R2][N4-F3][N5-R4]. The patient should be taught to recognize exacerbation signs, know when to seek medical help, and understand the importance of adherence to follow-up and home monitoring [N5-R3][N4-F3].

medication review and treatment recommendations for COPD

The evidence supports a clear distinction between inhaler classes, rescue medications, and COPD-specific treatment guidance. For inhalers, the evidence emphasizes that inhaled bronchodilators are the cornerstone of COPD treatment, either as initial/first-line treatment or for second-line treatment in patients with persistent symptoms or exacerbations [N3-F2]. It also notes that long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) and long-acting β2-agonists (LABAs) are important bronchodilator classes, with dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA) being recommended in patients with more severe symptoms [N3-F2]. Rescue medication review is also important because the evidence states that rescue bronchodilator therapy is recommended for all patients with stable COPD [N3-R2].

GOLD/ICS/LABA/LAMA guidance is central to COPD treatment. The evidence shows that the GOLD 2022 report recommends initial pharmacological treatment with a LAMA or LABA for most patients, and dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA/LAMA) for patients with more severe symptoms, regardless of exacerbation history [N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that the American Thoracic Society (ATS) guidelines strongly recommend LABA/LAMA combination therapy over LAMA or LABA monotherapy in patients with COPD and dyspnea or exercise intolerance [N3-F2]. # Integrated COPD SOAP note template

Here is a clinically focused COPD SOAP note template that includes the relevant clinical points for a new patient with advanced COPD. It integrates the branch reports’ evidence on structure, assessment, medication review, management, and patient education.

---

## 1. Standard SOAP note structure and how to adapt it for a COPD patient

A standard SOAP note is organized into four sections: **Subjective**, **Objective**, **Assessment**, and **Plan**. The evidence supports a goal-oriented scientific survey (GOSS) extension of the traditional SOAP note, which can help organize a COPD assessment more systematically by linking symptoms, diagnostics, and treatment decisions [N1-F1]. For a new COPD patient, the template should be adapted to capture COPD-specific elements such as GOLD classification, exacerbation risk, current disease control, comorbidities, and medication use, while also including functional status and home monitoring cues [N1-R3].

### Where to place the physician’s assessment and plan
The physician’s **assessment** should follow the **Subjective** and **Objective** sections, linking the findings to a diagnosis, staging, and treatment level. The **plan** should appear after the assessment and include medication, monitoring, education, and escalation cues [N1-F1][N1-R3].

---

## 2. Subjective section

### Chief complaint
- “Shortness of breath” or “dyspnea” is the primary concern [N2-R2][N2-R5].
- Other symptoms may include cough, sputum changes, fatigue, or worsening breathlessness with routine activities [N4-F3].

### History of present illness
- When did the shortness of breath start?
- How long has it lasted?
- Is it getting worse, or is it new?
- Are there changes in sputum production, color, or frequency?
- Any fever or other new symptoms?
- What activities bring on or worsen shortness of breath?
- Are there any recent infections or environmental exposures?
- Are there any medication changes, missed doses, or difficulty using inhalers?
- Any history of exacerbations, hospitalizations, or emergency visits?

### Past medical history
- COPD diagnosis, GOLD classification, and current disease control [N1-F1].
- History of asthma, eosinophilia, or frequent exacerbations [N3-F2].
- Comorbidities, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or others relevant to COPD management [N1-F1].

### Medication history
- Current inhalers, rescue medications, and any other prescribed medications [N3-R2][N3-R3].
- Adherence to current therapy, including missed doses or difficulty using devices [N3-R2][N3-R3].

### Smoking and exposures
- Tobacco use history, including pack-years and cessation status [N1-F1].
- Exposure to environmental irritants, allergens, or pollutants [N4-F3].

---

## 3. Objective section

### Vital signs
- Blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature, and oxygen saturation [N1-F1][N4-F3].
- Oxygen saturation should be recorded and compared to the patient’s baseline, especially if the provider suspects exacerbation [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### Physical examination
- Respiratory exam: wheezing, crackles, use of accessory muscles, respiratory distress, and altered mental status [N1-R1][N4-F3].
- Signs of hypercapnia: confusion, altered level of consciousness, or other indicators of respiratory failure [N4-F3].

### Pulmonary function and functional assessment
- Spirometry, PFTs, CAT score, and 6MWT results, if available [N1-F1].
- Any recent chest X-ray or other imaging relevant to the current episode [N1-F1].

### Laboratory or diagnostic findings
- Eosinophil count, if relevant to ICS eligibility [N3-F2].
- Other laboratory values that may affect management or exacerbation risk [N1-F1].

---

## 4. Assessment section

### Diagnosis and staging
- COPD with shortness of breath, likely worsening symptoms [N2-R2][N4-F3].
- GOLD classification and exacerbation risk status [N1-F1][N1-R3].
- Acute exacerbation suspicion if there is increased dyspnea, worsening sputum, or lower-than-usual oxygen levels [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### Severity and functional status
- Dyspnea severity and activity limitation should be quantified with validated tools rather than relying only on self-report [N1-F1][N2-R3].
- Functional limitation: reduced exercise tolerance, difficulty with routine activities, and impact on daily living [N3-F2].

### Medication review
- Current therapy should be evaluated for appropriateness, adherence, and any gaps [N3-R2][N3-R3].
- Rescue bronchodilator therapy should be checked, as it is recommended for all patients with stable COPD [N3-R2].

### Exacerbation risk
- Exacerbation risk is elevated if the patient has increased sputum production, changes in sputum color, or a history of frequent exacerbations [N4-F3].
- The patient may need an action plan for early recognition of worsening symptoms [N4-F3].

### Differential considerations
- Consider acute exacerbation, infection, or other respiratory causes if the clinical picture is unclear [N4-F3].

---

## 5. Plan section

### Treatment and medication plan
- **Inhalers and bronchodilators**: confirm current regimen and consider whether to optimize, escalate, or change therapy [N3-F2][N3-R2].
- **Rescue medication**: ensure the patient understands when and how to use rescue bronchodilators [N3-R2].
- **ICS use**: reserve ICS for patients with high eosinophil count, history of frequent exacerbations, or asthma [N3-F2]. Avoid ICS in patients who do not meet these criteria [N3-F2].
- **Triple therapy**: consider LABA/LAMA/ICS if dual bronchodilator therapy is inadequate [N3-R4][N6-R1].
- **Oxygen therapy**: titrate to achieve SaO2 >90% or PaO2 >60 mmHg, but avoid over-oxygenation in patients at risk for hypercapnia [N4-F3].

### Monitoring and follow-up
- Schedule follow-up in 1 week and arrange future PFTs or other monitoring as needed [N1-F1].
- Use routine follow-ups to ask about and monitor key clinical indicators, including spirometry values and changes in symptoms [N5-R4].

### Home monitoring plan
- Teach the patient to monitor oxygen saturation, symptom changes, and sputum characteristics [N4-F3][N5-R4].
- Provide a clear action plan for when symptoms worsen and what to do next [N4-F3].

### Patient education
- Educate on trigger avoidance, including tobacco smoke, allergens, air pollution, and environmental irritants [N4-F3][N5-R2].
- Teach the patient to recognize exacerbation signs and when to seek help [N5-R3][N4-F3].
- Emphasize adherence to prescribed medications and the importance of follow-up [N3-R2][N5-R4].

### Escalation cues
- Seek medical attention if there is worsening breathlessness, increased sputum, changes in sputum color, fever, confusion, altered mental status, or lower-than-usual oxygen levels [N4-F3].
- If symptoms become severe, consider hospitalization, IV steroids, nebulized bronchodilators, antibiotics, and oxygen support [N4-F3].
- The cited COPD SOAP note example includes empiric steroids and antibiotics for acute exacerbation, increasing bronchodilators, and follow-up in 1 week [N1-F1].

---

## 6. Sample COPD SOAP note template

### Subjective
- Chief complaint: Shortness of breath
- History of present illness: The patient reports worsening shortness of breath over the past [X] days. Symptoms are worse with routine activities, and they now notice increased cough and changes in sputum. They have no fever but feel more fatigued. They have been using their rescue inhaler more frequently.

- Smoking history: [X] pack-years, currently [X].
- Environmental exposures: [X].

### Objective
- Vital signs: BP [X], HR [X], RR [X], Temp [X], SaO2 [X]
- Respiratory exam: Wheezing, crackles, accessory muscle use, respiratory distress, confusion [X]
- Pulmonary function: CAT score [X], PFTs [X], 6MWT [X]
- Chest X-ray: [X]
- Other findings: [X]

### Assessment
- Diagnosis: COPD with worsening dyspnea
- GOLD classification: [X]
- Exacerbation risk: [X]
- Functional status: [X]
- Medication review: [X]
- Acute exacerbation suspicion: [X]
- Differential diagnosis: [X]

### Plan
- Inhalers/bronchodilators: [X]
- Rescue medication: [X]
- ICS use: [X]
- Triple therapy: [X]
- Oxygen therapy: [X]
- Follow-up: [X]
- Home monitoring: [X]
- Patient education: [X]
- Escalation cues: [X]

---

## 7. Clinical synthesis

This template is built on the branch reports’ evidence and should be tailored to the specific patient. For a new COPD patient, the note should emphasize:
- **Symptoms and severity indicators**: dyspnea, breathlessness, cough, sputum changes [N2-R2][N4-F3].
- **Functional status**: reduced exercise tolerance, difficulty with daily activities, and impact on quality of life [N3-F2].
- **Medication review**: current inhalers, rescue medications, adherence, and ICS eligibility [N3-R2][N3-F2].
- **Exacerbation recognition**: increased sputum, changes in sputum color, fatigue, confusion, and altered oxygen levels [N4-F3].
- **Oxygen management**: titrate to SaO2 >90% or PaO2 >60 mmHg, but be cautious of over-oxygenation [N4-F3].
- **Trigger avoidance and education**: teach the patient to avoid tobacco, allergens, and pollutants, and to recognize worsening signs [N4-F3][N5-R2].
- **Follow-up and escalation**: schedule routine follow-ups, teach home monitoring, and define clear next steps for worsening symptoms [N5-R4][N4-F3].

The evidence also supports using validated surveys and spirometry to quantify disease severity and response to treatment [N1-F1]. In practice, this SOAP note should be adapted to the patient’s baseline, exacerbation history, and current therapeutic context [N1-F1][N3-F2].

# Integrated COPD SOAP note template

Here is a clinically focused COPD SOAP note template that includes the relevant clinical points for a new patient with advanced COPD. It integrates the branch reports’ evidence on structure, assessment, medication review, management, and patient education.

## 1. Standard SOAP note structure and how to adapt it for a COPD patient

A standard SOAP note is organized into four sections: **Subjective**, **Objective**, **Assessment**, and **Plan**. For a new COPD patient, the template should be adapted to capture COPD-specific elements such as GOLD classification, exacerbation risk, current disease control, comorbidities, and medication use, while also including functional status and home monitoring cues [N1-R3].

### Where to place the physician’s assessment and plan
The physician’s **assessment** should follow the **Subjective** and **Objective** sections, linking the findings to a diagnosis, staging, and treatment level. The **plan** should appear after the assessment and include medication, monitoring, education, and escalation cues [N1-F1][N1-R3].

## 2. Subjective section

### Chief complaint
- “Shortness of breath” or “dyspnea” is the primary concern [N2-R2][N2-R5].
